ExplanationParts.CorpusEarnedOpening: a nest or mortar; in the Chan record, a fixed mould into which words and conduct settle.
EvidenceBody: The corpus speaks of falling into another's rut (墮他窠臼, "fall into his fixed rut") as oil enters flour and cannot get out, and of both inherited gestures and current fashions as ruts: "killing buddhas and patriarchs" falls within the old people's enclosure, while wielding the staff and shout does not escape the present-day rut (殺佛殺祖，盡落古人圜繢；行棒行喝，不脫今時窠臼). One record pairs new and old while saying "jump out of the rut" (一新一舊，跳出窠臼). The decisive corpus warning is recursive: pupils may mistake Yuanwu Keqin’s refusal to establish a rut and thereby make "no rut" into a rut (以無窠臼為窠臼, "take having no rut as a rut"). Thus the Chan deviation is not merely an ordinary habit: the term names repeatable religious speech, gestures, formats, and even anti-formulas once followers preserve them as a template.
